claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution.
The initial solid solution is homogeneous and contains no significant intermetallic precipitation.
High-temperature aging increases diffusion sufficiently to drive Mg segregation from the metastable solid solution.
Slight short-range ordering initiates the transformation.
Mg-rich nanoscale clusters rapidly nucleate during thermal exposure.
The Mg-rich clusters coalesce and act as precursors or nucleation sites for intermetallic compounds.
Continued exposure produces discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates through nucleation and growth.
Intermetallic precipitation depletes Mg locally from the remaining matrix.
The transformation produces a chemically and structurally heterogeneous microstructure.
Phase separation and local chemical changes compromise the integrity or maintenance of the protective passive film.
The transformation and associated surface-film disruption decrease high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aged samples will contain detectable discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the initial state.
The appearance of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates will correlate with measurable declines in electrochemical corrosion performance.
The appearance of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates will correlate with poorer cyclic high-temperature oxidation performance.
The initial homogeneous solid solution supports robust passive-film formation.
The proposed mechanism applies under oxidizing or corrosive high-temperature service conditions where diffusion is accelerated but the alloy remains below its melting point.
